Mars, where we have driven

A volcano, a canyon, five landing sites and a moon. Leaving goes back to Earth.

Open the trip: Mars, where we have driven

The red planet

Mars is half as wide as the Earth, and its day is forty minutes longer than ours. The red is rust: iron in the dust, which the wind spreads over the whole planet. Machines have been landing here for fifty years, and two rovers are still driving.

Olympus Mons

The largest volcano we know of on any planet. It is more than twenty kilometres high, and its base would cover Arizona. Mars has no moving plates, so the lava kept piling up in one place for a very long time.

Valles Marineris

A canyon nearly four thousand kilometres long, which on Earth would reach from one side of the United States to the other. In places it is nine kilometres deep. It began as a crack, when the volcanoes beside it swelled and the ground split.

The first to stay

Viking 1 landed here in the summer of 1976 and worked for six years. Its twin came down on the other side of the planet six weeks later. They tested the soil for life, and the answer was unclear. That is why we kept coming back.

Built for ninety days

Opportunity was built to last ninety Martian days. It drove forty-five kilometres in more than fourteen years, and found rocks that could only have formed in water. A dust storm that covered the whole planet ended it in 2018.

Curiosity, climbing a mountain

Curiosity is the size of a small car and runs on the heat of plutonium, so dust on solar panels cannot stop it. Since 2012 it has been climbing a mountain of layered rock in the middle of this crater, reading a wet Mars turning into a dry one.

InSight, listening

InSight never moved. It set a seismometer on the ground and listened, and heard more than thirteen hundred marsquakes. From the way they echoed, we know Mars has a core of liquid metal. Dust covered its solar panels, and it fell silent in 2022.

Perseverance, and a helicopter

Perseverance landed in this crater in 2021, where a river once ran into a lake. It is filling tubes with rock for a later mission to bring home. It carried a small helicopter, Ingenuity, which made seventy-two flights: the first powered flights on another world.

Phobos, and Deimos

Mars has two small moons shaped like potatoes. This is Phobos, about twenty-two kilometres across, so close in that it goes round three times a day. Deimos is half the size and further out. Phobos is slowly falling: in some fifty million years it will break up, or hit Mars.

Ice, and seasons

Mars is tilted about as much as the Earth, so it has seasons, each nearly twice as long as ours. Every winter part of its thin air freezes onto the pole as dry-ice frost, and every spring it blows away again. Under the frost is a cap of water ice.

Everything is drawn where it really is, from published star and galaxy catalogues.
